title: TikTok as a platform for hysteroscopy information: An analytical video-based cross-sectional study to assess quality, reliability, and accuracy
screen_reason: Unlike a pure quality-instrument study, this paper carries a separate, explicitly veracity-based misinformation assessment alongside its quality scales: every one of the 144 included TikTok 'hysteroscopy' videos was fact-checked by expert gynecologists against accepted hysteroscopy guidelines and the existing literature and placed in one of three bands defined by the PROPORTION OF FALSE INFORMATION it contained (>50% false = 'inaccurate or misinformative'; 25-50% = 'partially accurate'; <25% = 'accurate and evidence-based'). Table 2 reports the resulting counts and shares with their denominator, so a CONTENT prevalence estimate exists. The PEMAT A/V, mDISCERN, GQS and VIQI results in the same paper are QUALITY scale scores and are not extracted as prevalence.

estimates.country: Not restricted; creator locations reported as North America 97 (67.4%), Europe 24 (16.7%), Asia 12 (8.3%), Africa 8 (5.6%), Oceania 3 (2.1%); English-language (or audio-free) videos only
estimates.measure_type: % of English-language TikTok videos about hysteroscopy judged 'inaccurate or misinformative', i.e. containing more than 50% false information
estimates.value_raw: 50 (34.7) of 144 videos 'Inaccurate or uninformative'; the other bands were 'Partially accurate' 63 (43.8) and 'Accurate and evidence-based' 31 (21.5)
estimates.denominator: 144 TikTok videos with hysteroscopy as their main focus and in English (or audio-free), retained from the 300 videos returned for the keyword 'hysteroscopy' (156 excluded: 101 off-topic, 49 non-English, 1 removed from the platform, 5 duplicates)
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if expert fact-checking judged that more than 50% of the information it presented was false; verification was against accepted hysteroscopy guidelines and the existing literature. Videos with 25-50% false information were placed in a separate 'partially accurate' band and are NOT in this numerator.
estimates.misinfo_def: "The misinformation level within the videos was categorized as follows: content that included more than 50% false information was classified as 'inaccurate or misinformative'; videos containing less than 50% but more than 25% false information were classified as 'partially accurate'; videos containing less than 25% misinformation were labeled as 'accurate and evidence-based.'"

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Expert clinician coding: "a team composed of one senior gynecologist (SGV) who had performed more than 500 diagnostic and operative hysteroscopic procedures and two residents in Obstetrics and Gynecology (GS and SS)" independently and simultaneously scored every video; "Discrepancies in the assessment were addressed by an additional gynecologist (GR)", producing a unified consensus. Fact-checking was "conducted utilizing accepted guidelines for hysteroscopy and data from the existing literature." No kappa or other inter-rater reliability coefficient is reported anywhere in the paper.

estimates.notes: borderline=true because the band's LABEL and its DEFINITION do not match: the Methods define it purely by falsity (>50% false information), but Table 2, the Results text and the abstract all call it 'inaccurate or uninformative', and uninformative content need not be false. If uninformative videos were folded into this band, the 34.7% is an upper bound on the >50%-false share; the Methods definition is what I coded, hence breadth=false. Kept the strict band as the row. The 'any false content' figure (43.8% + 34.7% = 78.5%) is a cross-category sum I would have had to compute and is barred by R8, so it is not extracted - an adjudicator wanting a broad-definition row must take that decision explicitly. denom_scope=topical with denom_selection=curated: a single keyword, rank-truncated at the first 300 algorithmically ordered results. country_norm=Global: no country filter, creators spread across five continents, though two thirds are North American and the English-only rule biases the sample. No inter-rater reliability is reported for any instrument, which is the main threat to this estimate. Quote note: this PDF is two-column and the -layout rendering interleaves the two columns on every line, so no multi-sentence prose span is contiguous in the text file. source_quote is therefore the Table 2 misinformation block, which is contiguous; the columns are Overall (144) / Healthcare workers (50) / Patients (94), and the rendering splits the patients cell of the 'Partially accurate' row so that '43 (45.7)' appears as a stray '4' followed by '3 (45.7)'. The prose statement of the same result reads 'Concerning the misinformation about hysteroscopic content on TikTok, most of the content was considered partially accurate or uninformative (63 [43.8%] and 50 [34.7%], respectively).' moderator_quote is truncated to one line for the same reason; the full sentence continues 'keyword “hysteroscopy.” A new account was created for this research to mitigate the influence of algorithmically personalized content.'

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) The creator subgroup split of the same 144 videos, which is a headline in the abstract: inaccurate or uninformative 48/94 (51.1%) for patient creators vs 2/50 (4.0%) for healthcare workers; partially accurate 43/94 (45.7%) vs 20/50 (40%); accurate and evidence-based 3/94 (3.2%) vs 28/50 (56%). These are subgroups of the corpus already represented by the pooled row, and the instruction is to keep the main figure rather than subgroup rows, so they are recorded here in full for an adjudicator who wants a creator-type moderator cell (note the two subgroups have different population_scope: patients = general_public, healthcare workers = professional). (b) The 'partially accurate' band alone, 63/144 (43.8%) - a middle band (25-50% false), neither the strict nor a broad prevalence reading, so keeping it as a row would misrepresent it as a prevalence figure. (c) All QUALITY-instrument results, which are scale scores and not shares: PEMAT A/V understandability median 42.9% (IQR 11.1-70.0) and actionability median 0% (IQR 0-0); mDISCERN median 1 (IQR 0-2); VIQI total median 7 (IQR 4-11) with subscales flow 2, information accuracy 2, quality 2, precision 2; GQS median 1 (IQR 1-3), plus every professional-vs-patient split of these (e.g. understandability 60.0% vs 33.3%, mDISCERN 2 vs 1, VIQI 11 vs 5, GQS 2 vs 1). Note in particular that 'VIQI 2 information accuracy' is an accuracy-flavoured item but is reported only as a median score, so the 'Likert accuracy scale reported only as a mean is not a share' rule applies. (d) Table 2 codes that are tone or effect rather than veracity, so not misinformation prevalence: suggests hysteroscopy is painful 25 (17.4%), encourages patients to avoid hysteroscopy 6 (4.2%), encourages distrust of their gynecologist 11 (7.6%), increases anxiety/concern 25 (17.4%), describes alternatives 6 (4.2%). Pain and anxiety content is not false information (hysteroscopy can be painful), so none of these belongs in a numerator. (e) Corpus composition figures: 50/144 (34.7%) videos by healthcare providers vs 94/144 (65.3%) by patients (the paper mislabels these as 25.5% and 74.5% in the text while Table 1 and Table 2 both use n = 50 and n = 94 - an internal error worth flagging), video category shares (medical education 62 (43.1%), storytelling 67 (46.5%)), tone shares, and creator locations. These describe who posts, not what is true. (f) The off-topic breakdown of excluded videos (of 101 off-topic, 56 (55.4%) other gynecologic topics, 4 (4.0%) obstetrical, 4 (4.0%) non-gynecologic endoscopy, 39 (38.6%) unrelated medical) is a search-precision statistic, not a misinformation share. (g) Engagement medians and Spearman correlations - not shares.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis, no human participants (IRB approval not required; all content publicly available). Single keyword 'hysteroscopy' searched on TikTok on 13 January 2024 from a newly created account to blunt personalisation; results taken in the platform's default algorithmic order without filtration; 300 videos screened, 144 included, 156 excluded (101 off-topic, 49 non-English, 1 removed from platform, 5 duplicates); inclusion required hysteroscopy as the main focus and English or audio-free presentation. Metadata extracted manually into a standardised spreadsheet (title, duration, description, upload date, hashtags, location, views, likes, shares, comments, creator followers and totals); creators classified as healthcare professionals (physicians, nurses, midwives, medical students) or patients. Coding by one senior gynecologist with >500 hysteroscopies plus two OB/GYN residents, independently and simultaneously, with a fourth gynecologist adjudicating discrepancies to consensus; NO inter-rater reliability statistic is reported. Instruments: PEMAT A/V (17 items), mDISCERN (5 items), GQS (1-5), VIQI (four 5-point criteria), plus the bespoke three-band misinformation scale fact-checked against accepted hysteroscopy guidelines and the literature. Statistics: Shapiro-Wilk, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's test, Spearman correlations, STATA 14.1, alpha 0.05. No funding, no conflicts. Authors' stated limitations: the rating team was composed only of gynecology professionals with no patient representation, the single search term missed videos tagged differently, and TikTok's keyword sensitivity may have skewed which settings, creator backgrounds and content categories were represented. Sample is English-only and two-thirds North American.
